newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Airborne daredevils could become "sky flyers".
newsitem.headline: Airborne daredevils could become "sky flyers".

text.p: Would-be daredevils who cannot stomach bungee jumping may prove gutsy enough to have a crack at a more controllable airborne thrill -- sky flying.
Sky flying, as launched by Belgian games company Benji Fun Belgium, involves a crane, a long wire, a propellor and a man.

The flyer is dangled 15 meters (yards) off the ground, clutching a motorised fan which he can steer so that he virtually flies from a steel cable attached to a crane on a truck at speeds of up to 30 km (18 miles) an hour.

"It's hard on your arms and with high winds it's really tough, but what a great feeling it gives you," said a Belgian television presenter at this week's launch, delayed for two hours due to blustery conditions.

"It's not walking, it's not jumping or running, to me it's flying," said Stefan Kerkhofs, the head of Benji Fun, which has developed a series of airborne thrills, mostly of the slingshot type involving thick, long rubber bands.
The company, set up seven years ago, gradually started renting out variations on bungee jumping to clients across Europe for entertainment events.
"We want to give clients something new every time," said Kerkhofs, who is preparing for the summer season with hot air-rides.

One of his new machines enables amateur stuntmen to float aloft, pushed up by air propelled from 12-cylinder turbo engine lying flat on the soil and surrounded by airbags and a metal cage to help them to stay on course.
Another act is the reverse bungee jump, catapulting people attached to a bungee cord into the air.
The company hires out its equipment -- enabling the brave to experience a total of 14 attactions -- at a daily rate of 50,000 ($1,450) to 200,000 Belgian francs.
"For our next project a client sits on top of a 20-meter high flexible pole, attached to the ground, which swings and spins around in all directions," Kerkhofs said.
